chapter_theme: Sivavakkiyar sets the priest's purity against itself (Brahmins who shun fish yet bathe in fish-water, who shun goat yet sacrifice it; gods knotted in cloth; water poured into water) and puts in its place a Lord found in the body: the blue lamp at the brow, the five letters climbed as a ladder from NA and MA to SI, the breath as the great light, and ciphered counts of the body's centres. The refrain சிவாயம் (Sivayam) closes question after question about where body, breath and desire were before they were.
structure_note: Not an arranged chapter: the tool's running cut of a long work under one editorial heading (அறிவு நிலை). Still, the stanzas fall into runs: questions and fables of the body's end (1114 to 1120); the attack on Brahmin purity (1121 to 1123); the Lord within and the five letters (1124 to 1130); the triple question of what was before conception, with its answer (1131, 1132); abuse of the jnani and a riddle (1133, 1134); and number-ciphers on the body ending in the fifty-one letters and the lion-roar (1135 to 1138).

1114.reading: When sleep comes and forgets the books recited, the learning understood, wife, children and kin, where did they go and hide, or did they stand become everywhere? Tell me, Lord, the mystery of their hiding in the light.
1114.nuance: Sleep is used as a test: whatever vanishes nightly, learning and family alike, cannot be what one is. The last line offers two answers in the form of a question, that they hid somewhere or that they became everything, and leaves both open. 1172 repeats the stanza with mantras and Agamas in place of books.

1115.reading: Like bundles hung on the neck of a buffalo that has calved, you fools knot him up in three or four cloths; the endless Lord who is the three and four worlds, what truth is there in the god you have bound up?
1115.nuance: The target is a god wrapped in cloth, an image or an amulet, set against a Lord who is the worlds themselves. ஈணெருமை is a buffalo that has calved (ஈன்ற எருமை); ஊணிஊணி is unclear, perhaps ஊன்றி ஊன்றி (pressing tight) or a word for tying. மூணுநாலு (three-four) is used twice, of cloths and of worlds, and the second may simply mean 'all the worlds'.

1116.reading: Four cocks and five chicks, as though one brood, quarrel together in the guarded coop; once the old jackal has got into the coop, all four and all five are dead.
1116.nuance: A fable in cipher. The plain reading is a body whose contents squabble until death enters. The numbers carry the coded sense: tradition takes the four as the inner faculties (mind, intellect, will, ego) or the four Vedas, the five as the senses, the coop as the body and the old jackal as death. கூவமான் in line 3 is obscure and may be a corrupt word.

1117.reading: If you rise at dawn and cut the four bindings of the sedge sprouting in the root pond, you can live as a child and become the supreme Brahman; the feet of the poison-eating Lord and the Mother's feet are the truth.
1117.nuance: The root pond (மூலக் குளம்) is, in tradition, the muladhara, and the sedge that sprouts there the coiled power or the desires rooted in it; the four bindings are not fixed (the four faculties, or four states). காலமே means 'early' but also plays on கால், breath. The plain reading, weeding a pond at dawn, stands on its own as an image of daily discipline.

1118.reading: As layers of verdigris form on copper, so the light of the beautiful hall, which cannot be written down, is covered; heat it and heat it until it thins and merges upward, and see how the copper has shed its tarnish.
1118.nuance: The gloss takes அணியரங்கம் as the little hall at Chidambaram, so the light is the dancing Lord's, here inside the self. வெம்பி (burning, grieving) is the discipline, and the simile is also the alchemist's: tarnish burnt off copper. அம்பினில் எழுதொணாத is unclear, perhaps 'cannot be written in water' (அம்பு). Compare 1145, where the tarnish is cut from gold.

1119.reading: If you can seek and seek and gaze with love within yourselves, the one who runs out and runs back will settle within you; even Death who came hunting will stand bewildered and go, and you will remain without lack for crores of ages.
1119.nuance: ஓடிஓடி மீளுவான், the one who runs out and returns, is not named: the breath, the mind, or the Lord himself all fit, and the practice differs with each. The promise of life without lack for crores of ages is the Siddhar's claim of deathlessness, taken by some as the body's and by others as the soul's.

1120.reading: What are you quarrelling about, fools who have lost awareness? You do not know the great light that never quarrels, the prana. If you can cut the knot of the two quarrelling deeds, you can have the great joy that does not quarrel.
1120.nuance: The breath itself is named the great light (பேரொளி பிராணன்), which is the Siddhars' identification rather than a simile. பிணங்கு (quarrel, tangle) opens every line; the two deeds are good and bad karma, and the verse asks for their knot to be cut, not for good deeds to outweigh bad.

1121.reading: The Brahmins say they have never eaten fish, then or now; but the water they dive in and drink is where the fish live. They say they have never eaten deer; but the thread on their chest hangs from a stripped deer's hide.
1121.nuance: The argument is not that one should eat flesh; it is that the purity rule cannot be kept by anyone who bathes or wears the thread, so purity of birth and diet is incoherent. The deer-skin (கிருஷ்ணாஜினம்) is worn with the sacred thread by the initiated.

1122.reading: Brahmins have never eaten goat, then or now; but is not the sacrifice you perform goat-flesh? They have never eaten cow; but is not what you put into your vegetable dish from the cow?
1122.nuance: The sacrifice (யாகம்) is called goat-flesh outright, which turns the Vedic rite into butchery. The last line is less clear: what from the cow goes into the vegetable dish may be ghee and milk, or dung used as fuel; either way the cow's body is being consumed.

1123.reading: A string of jibes built on rhyme: you wear the rudraksha for the one who stands as the beginning of all lives; you strain and press; you blacken yourselves, being born and dying and dying again; you gorge; and what I have made you understand is the truth.
1123.nuance: Each line opens with a slang verb (அக்கு இடீர், முக்கு இடீர், மைக்கு இடீர், மொக்கு இடீர்): wear the bead, strain, put on black, gulp. அக்கு is the rudraksha bead; முக்கு is to strain or to dip; மை may be kohl or the darkness of ignorance. உமைப்பிடித்து முத்தரித்து is obscure (seizing Uma, bearing three?). The sense is a mockery of outward religion, but the lines cannot be fixed word by word.

1124.reading: How did the Lord come and enter the true inner self? As water enters the tender coconut on the red palm. And once the Lord has entered and made the body his temple, there is no more opening the mouth to the people of the world.
1124.nuance: The coconut's water appears inside with no visible door, which answers the 'how' by denying any entrance to watch for. The fruit of the Lord's dwelling is silence toward the world, not preaching, which sits oddly beside a poet who preaches in every stanza.

1125.reading: Passing beyond NA and MA, resting on the SI that cannot be sought, with VA and YA within it as the generous teaching of wisdom, the Shakti filling within and piercing through the crown: those who know this way are, I swear by the Lord, the Lord himself.
1125.nuance: The five letters are climbed as a ladder: NA and MA (in Siddhanta reading the Lord's concealing power and impurity) are left behind, SI (Siva) is the ground, VA (grace, Shakti) and YA (the soul) are found within it. That assignment is the tradition's, as in Tirumanthiram 975; the verse itself only names the letters and the crown. ஒவ்வு சத்தி, the matching Shakti, may be the power of grace or the kundalini that pierces the crown.

1126.reading: Is the letter beginningless? Is the soul beginningless? Are the elements and senses that have entered us beginningless? Are the books full of argument and the shastras beginningless? Is the true guru who cut through to the Supreme beginningless?
1126.nuance: Five questions, no answer. Saiva Siddhanta holds the soul and its bonds beginningless, and the guru's grace too; set as questions beside letter, elements and books, the doctrine is made to defend itself. 1173 repeats the stanza with Sadasiva in the guru's place.

1127.reading: What is it you saw? Whatever is looked at perishes in the looking; if you stay keen, Siva is in the inner intent. Whenever you look, leave the looking itself behind, and you will join like the flower that has bloomed with its fruit.
1127.nuance: குறிப்பில் அச்சிவமதாம் places Siva in the intent or sign, below the act of seeing. The last word, பிறப்பிரே, is odd: 'you who are born' as address, or 'you will be born', which would reverse the sense; the flower-and-fruit image suggests ripening rather than rebirth.

1128.reading: Hold in devotion the great blue lamp that flickers at the brow, stand and stand there until attachment is cut: that is the fruit. Stay joined and look: above the inner light there is a light beyond, and the one who knows where the Father sits is himself beginningless.
1128.nuance: The blue lamp (நீல விளக்கு) at the forehead is, in yogic tradition, the light seen at the brow centre in meditation; the verse does not explain it. உள்ஒளிக்கு மேல்ஒளி, a light above the inner light, ranks the vision below what it leads to. The last line makes the knower, not only the Lord, beginningless. 1130 repeats the image.

1129.reading: You scoop up water and pour it back into water: what do you think you have done, and whom are you thinking of as you pour it all out in vain? If you can think on the root, on the seed, and on the glory that sprouts from the seed, you may reach Siva's state.
1129.nuance: The rite is the water-offering (tarpana, ablution) done in a river. The verse does not ask for a better rite but for thought (உன்னல்) on root and seed, the source of things; சிவபதங்கள் may be Siva's feet or Siva's state. 1175 asks the same question in its first line.

1130.reading: Discern and look at the blue lamp that wavers at the forehead, the light that stands within; those who followed it in devotion have become the Supreme itself, and those who dwell in that place are my masters.
1130.nuance: Near-repeat of 1128, with the result stated: those who follow the inner light become the Supreme (பரமயம்), and the poet calls them his masters (நாதர்), the only place in these stanzas where he bows to anyone.

1131.reading: Before conception, where did the body stand? Before it took form, where did the breath stand? Before grace was received, where did desire stand? Say that Sivayam is what has cut this knot of doubt.
1131.nuance: The gloss on 1132 gives திருக்கு as doubt, so the refrain line says the mantra cuts doubt rather than that it is twisted. Three befores (body, breath, desire) are set against three afters (conception, form, grace). 1132 answers; 1185 asks again with different answers.

1132.reading: The answers: before conception the body was in fire; before form, in fire again; before grace, desire was in the wind; and say that Sivayam is what has cut the doubt.
1132.nuance: Line 2 repeats காயம் and தேயு from line 1 where 1131's question was about the breath (உயிர்ப்பு), so the text is probably doubled by a copyist and the second answer lost. Fire and wind as the pre-states of body and desire follow the Siddhars' element-physiology; the verse gives no account of where grace was.

1133.reading: The dasas and the Saivas of the place, with the children of the outcaste woman, acting together, hurried to throw stones at the jnani walking down the street; what it yielded them was sin, by Sivayam.
1133.nuance: தாதர் (dasas) are the Vaishnava devotees, set beside Saivas; both sects join in stoning the knower. Line 2 is hard: கூதரைப் பறைச்சி மக்கள் may be the sectarians' own slur for the jnani's companions, or the poet's way of saying that high sect and low birth are alike in this. The event may be the poet's own experience, and the refrain closes the verse as a verdict.

1134.reading: The soles whitened from running and running about in sin; the wretched cat came and leapt into the milk; the pandit came and looked and said 'nothing to it'; and the thread snapped. What illusion is this, Lord?
1134.nuance: A riddle stanza. Plainly read, it is a life wasted and ended, with the astrologer's verdict that nothing could be done. In the coded reading tradition offers, the milk is the inner nectar or the seed, the cat the mind or desire that spoils it, the thread the breath that snaps at death. பணிக்கன் is a teacher or astrologer.

1135.reading: A cipher of counts: four for the square, eight for the Vedas, three for the fire, six for the wind in its circle, eight for the mountains of blood, all reckoned above my head: this is the nada that mingled and rose in the radiant body.
1135.nuance: The numbers are read by tradition as the body's centres: the square of four as the four-petalled root lotus, the six of wind as the six-petalled centre above it, the fire's three as the three-angled centre at the navel, the count ending above the head as the ascent to the crown. The mapping is not secure, and 'eight mountains of blood' has no settled sense. What the verse states plainly is that sound arises in the body when the count is complete.

1136.reading: Four and six, ten; then four and three; then ten and six above, gathered into one: when the guru sits within the circled five letters and tells it, the sheath that appeared as skin, body and sound is known.
1136.nuance: The sums (ten, seven, sixteen, one) are the Siddhars' arithmetic, taken by tradition as the ten airs or channels and the sixteen kalas gathered into the one. கோசம் (kosha, sheath) is the body as a covering; the verse says it is known only when told by a guru, from within the mantra, which is as much as the poet will reveal. 1137 carries கோசம் on.

1137.reading: What rose as the sheath, what stood piercing the cage of the body, what was born as the land, is Sivayam, the five letters; the countless mantras are for the Lord to drink, and the fifty-one letters stand filling the vessel.
1137.nuance: The fifty-one letters are the Sanskrit alphabet, the matrikas of mantra theory; the verse ranks them below the five, which are what rose, pierced and was born. ஈசனார் அருந்திட (for the Lord to drink) is odd and may mean the mantras are offered to him; ஆசயம் (vessel, receptacle) may be the body or the heart.

1138.reading: The pedestal of the linga in the body, the twice-five letters, the swelling lotus and the heart of those who join, the light that takes its share there, the five letters spread abroad and the lion-roar sound: nothing is other than Sivayam.
1138.nuance: அங்கலிங்க பீடம் makes the body the linga's pedestal, as the Lingayats also say. ஐயிரண்டு எழுத்து may be ten letters or 'the five and the two'. சிங்கநாத ஓசை, the lion's roar, is in yogic tradition one of the inner sounds heard when the breath is stilled. 1170 repeats the stanza with ajapa's three letters and conch and discus in place of the ten letters and the lotus.

links.note: 1172 repeats 1114 almost word for word, replacing the recited books and learning of line 1 with the cherished mantras and the Agamas (ஆதரித்த மந்திரம் அமைந்த ஆகமங்களும்). Together the two stanzas put secular learning and sacred scripture under the same test: both vanish in sleep.

Both are fables of creatures busy inside an enclosure while death waits: the Naladiyar's turtle plays in the pot with the fire lit beneath, Sivavakkiyar's cocks and chicks quarrel in the guarded coop until the old jackal gets in. The Naladiyar names its moral (Death waits his moment); Sivavakkiyar leaves the coop and jackal unexplained.

Both use tarnish on metal for the covering over the self. In 1118 verdigris on copper is burnt off by heating until the light of the hall shows; in 1145 the tarnish is cut from red gold and the god within is known that day. The metal changes from copper to gold, and the means from heating to cutting.

Kural 269 says leaping past Death becomes possible for those with the power of austerity (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும் கைகூடும்). 1119 says Death who came hunting is bewildered and goes for those who can see within themselves (தேடிவந்த காலனும் திகைத்திருந்து போய்விடும்). Both make a discipline, not a god's favour, the thing that turns Death away; the Kural's is tapas, Sivavakkiyar's inward seeing.

Both make the pair of deeds the knot to be undone before release. Tirumular has the two deeds balance (இருவினை ஒப்பு) so that grace can enter and impurity leave; Sivavakkiyar asks for the knot of the two quarrelling deeds to be cut (இருவினைப் பிணக்கறுக்க) so that the unquarrelling joy can be had. One word is balance, the other cutting, but the end is the same.

Tirumular says those without truth, knowledge, restraint and devotion are not Brahmins, whatever they are called. Sivavakkiyar shows the outward rule failing from the other side: the Brahmin who shuns fish bathes in fish-water and wears deer-hide. Both deny that purity of diet and emblem makes the Brahmin; Tirumular supplies the inner standard, Sivavakkiyar only the exposure.

Kural 259 ranks not killing one creature above pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). 1122 says the sacrifice the Brahmins perform is itself goat-flesh (ஆட்டிறைச்சி அல்லவோ யாகம்). The Kural compares merits and leaves the rite standing; Sivavakkiyar calls the rite killing and the priests' meat-rule a lie.

Tirumular says he once held the body a thing of shame, then saw the true substance within it and now cherishes it as the Highest's temple. Sivavakkiyar says the Lord entered the true inner self as water enters a tender coconut and took the body as his temple (கோயில் கொண்டபின்). Both make the body the temple by the Lord's dwelling; Sivavakkiyar adds silence toward the world as the consequence.

Tirumanthiram 975 assigns the five letters: SI is Siva, VA the form, YA the soul, and MA impurity. 1125 turns the assignment into a path: pass beyond NA and MA, rest on SI, find VA and YA within it as the teaching of wisdom, and the Shakti pierces the crown. What is a table of meanings in Tirumular becomes an order of ascent in Sivavakkiyar.

Tirumanthiram 2236 states as doctrine that the soul is beginningless and bound by five impurities that came without beginning (அனாதியே). 1126 asks the same of letter, soul, elements, books and guru (அனாதியோ?) and gives no answer. Sivavakkiyar turns what Tirumular asserts into open questions, and sets scripture and guru among the things questioned.

Both rank inner lamps. Tirumular's root lamp, seen lamp and higher lamp (மேலை விளக்கு) lead to release; Sivavakkiyar's blue lamp at the brow is held until, above the inner light, a higher light (உள்ஒளிக்கு மேல்ஒளி) is seen. In both the first light seen is not the last.

Tirumanthiram 510 says those who know only bathing cannot join the Lord, who is within the minds of those whose knowledge is clear. 1129 says scooping water and pouring it into water is done in vain, and that thought on the root and seed reaches Siva's state. Both set the water rite below inner knowing; Sivavakkiyar's tone is mockery, Tirumular's a ranking.

1131 asks where body, breath and desire stood before conception, form and grace; 1132 answers, body in fire and desire in wind, with the same refrain that Sivayam cuts the doubt. Read together they show the refrain working as the answer to any question, since 1131 already closes with it before the answer is given.

Tirumular says those who did evil to the ascetics who taught the one-syllable mantra will be born as outcaste dogs and outcastes in a hundred forms. Sivavakkiyar says the sectarians who stoned the jnani in the street reaped sin (பாதகங்கள் ஆகவே பலித்ததே). Both make abuse of the knower a sin that returns on the abuser; Tirumular names the return as low birth, which is the very slur Sivavakkiyar's stanza puts in the abusers' mouths.

Tirumanthiram 965 says the fifty letters are all the Vedas and Agamas, and once known they go and become the five letters. 1137 says what rose as sheath, pierced the body and was born as the land is the five letters, while the fifty-one letters stand filling the vessel. Both rank the whole alphabet of mantra below the five syllables; Sivavakkiyar counts fifty-one where Tirumular counts fifty.

1170 repeats 1138 with its middle changed: the ten letters become ajapa's three letters, the swelling lotus becomes conch and discus and all the sky, and the heart of those who join becomes the yogis who took a share and the five supreme gates. The frame (the body-linga's pedestal, the lion-roar, nothing but Sivayam) is the same, so the variable middle shows what the poet counted as interchangeable.

source_issues: 1132 line 2 (உருத்தரிக்கு முன்னெலாம் காயம்நின்ற தேயுவில்) repeats line 1's answer where 1131's question was about the breath (உயிர்ப்பு); probably a copyist's doubling, with the breath's answer lost.
1116 line 3 கூவமான் is obscure and may be corrupt.
1123 line 2 முத்தரித்து விட்டது cannot be construed; the stanza's slang verbs (அக்கிடீர், முக்கிடீர், மைக்கிடீர், மொக்கிடீர்) are read by guess.
1128 line 3 உற்றிருநது for உற்றிருந்து and line 4 அரிந்தவன் for அறிந்தவன் are spelling slips in the source.
1130 line 3 பத்தியில் தொடர்ந்தவர் is probably பத்தியிற் தொடர்ந்தவர்; no change of sense.
